naxp

Dealing with postcodes, flight numbers and other alphanumeric data codes is a common problem. Handling strings is cumbersome and the codes themselves can often be written in multiple different ways – for instance EC1A1BB and EC1A 1BB are the same UK postcode.

A naxp (‘encoded ASCII expression’) simplifies this by encoding each distinct alphanumeric data code as an integer.

With a naxp, you define the code system once using a flexible regex-like syntax, and then you’re done. Every naxp library, in every language (R, C, C++, C# and JavaScript), produces exactly the same encoding, which means that the encoded values are safe to store in files, to use in databases, and to pass between different programs written in different languages. And, as an added bonus, integers are more performant than strings.

The naxp website provides everything you need to understand and write naxps:

  • A good place to start is the naxp quick tour.

  • For common use cases, there are built-in standard naxps, which can be accessed direct from the R naxp package.

  • The site also has an interactive naxp design tool and a naxp migration tester.

Installation

Install from CRAN:

install.packages("naxp")

Or install the latest development version from GitHub:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("logmu-org/r-naxp")

Example 

library(naxp)

# Assume we have some UK postcodes
postcodes_as_text <- c(
  "CR2 6XH",
  "DN55 1PT",
  "M1 1AE",
  "EC1A1BB", # The mandated space is sometimes omitted
  "not a postcode")

# UK postcodes are complicated so let's grab the standard naxp
postcode_naxp <- naxp_standard("uk-postcode")
postcode_naxp
#> <naxp> \A\A?\9\X? \s!! \9\A\A | GIR \s!! 0AA
#> Maximum encoded value: 1755842401

# Encode the text postcodes
postcodes <- naxp_encode(postcodes_as_text, postcode_naxp)

# The encoded result looks like text ...
postcodes
#> <naxp_encoded[5]> \A\A?\9\X? \s!! \9\A\A | GIR \s!! 0AA
#> [1] CR2 6XH       DN55 1PT      M1 1AE        EC1A 1BB      <invalid (0)>

# ... but the underlying values are numerical,
# with 0 (not NA!) representing invalid text.
as.integer(postcodes)
#> [1] 180591302 238906246 743107201 277958384         0

# We can recover the canonical text form at any time.
# 0 (invalid text) decodes to NA.
naxp_decode(postcodes)
#> [1] "CR2 6XH"  "DN55 1PT" "M1 1AE"   "EC1A 1BB" NA
